slides.title: Chapter 12: Curvature and Topology
slides.notes: Frame the whole chapter as one question: what does local curvature force about global shape? Curvature is computed in a single tangent plane, yet it dictates whether a manifold can be compact, whether its universal cover is Euclidean space, and how large its fundamental group can be. The four signpost theorems are Killing-Hopf for constant curvature, Cartan-Hadamard for nonpositive curvature, Bonnet-Myers and Synge for positive curvature. Tell students every result here trades an inequality on K for a topological conclusion.

slides.title: The Curvature to Topology Program
slides.notes: The engine behind every theorem in the chapter is the Jacobi equation. A Jacobi field measures the separation of an infinitesimally nearby geodesic, and its second derivative is controlled by the curvature term. When K is negative this term pushes Jacobi fields to grow, so geodesics diverge and never refocus, which is why there are no conjugate points. When K is positive the term pulls geodesics back together, creating conjugate points within a bounded distance, and that bounded distance is exactly what forces compactness in Bonnet-Myers. Make sure students see that the diagram is the qualitative solution of an ODE.

slides.title: Constant Curvature: Space Forms and Killing-Hopf
slides.notes: Constant curvature is the cleanest case and sets the template for everything else. Killing-Hopf says the universal cover is rigidly determined by the sign of the constant: round sphere, flat space, or hyperbolic space, each unique up to scaling. Every complete connected space form is then one of these three models quotiented by a discrete group of isometries acting freely and properly discontinuously. Stress the word freely: the group must have no fixed points, otherwise the quotient is not a manifold. This reframes the classification as group-theoretic, for example flat tori and Klein bottles as quotients of R^n, and lens spaces as quotients of the sphere.

slides.title: Nonpositive Curvature: Cartan-Hadamard
slides.notes: Cartan-Hadamard is the headline result for nonpositive curvature. The key fact is that K nonpositive rules out conjugate points along any geodesic, so the exponential map has nonsingular differential everywhere; combined with completeness this makes exp_p a covering map onto M. The universal cover is therefore diffeomorphic to the tangent space R^n, and if M is already simply connected the exponential map itself is a global diffeomorphism. Emphasize the logical order: completeness gives surjectivity through Hopf-Rinow, absence of conjugate points gives the local diffeomorphism, and together they yield the covering.

slides.title: Consequences for pi_1 and Aspherical Spaces
slides.notes: This slide harvests the topological dividends of Cartan-Hadamard. Because the universal cover is contractible, the manifold is aspherical: every higher homotopy group vanishes and the entire homotopy type is encoded by the fundamental group. Such spaces are Eilenberg-MacLane spaces K(pi,1). A second consequence is that pi_1 must be torsion-free, because a deck transformation of finite order would have a fixed point on R^n by a center-of-mass argument, contradicting free action. The closed hyperbolic surface of genus two is the canonical example.

slides.title: Positive Curvature: Bonnet-Myers
slides.notes: Bonnet-Myers only needs a positive lower bound on Ricci curvature, not full sectional positivity, which makes it powerful. The proof is a second-variation argument: along any geodesic longer than pi over root kappa you can build a variation field that decreases length, so such a geodesic cannot be minimizing, which caps the diameter. Bounded diameter plus completeness gives compactness through Hopf-Rinow. The fundamental-group corollary is elegant: the universal cover inherits the same Ricci bound and is therefore also compact, but a compact cover can only cover a base finitely many times, so pi_1 is finite.

slides.title: Synge's Theorem: Orientability and Parity
slides.notes: Synge's theorem extracts orientability and simple connectivity from positive sectional curvature, and the proof is a gem of second-variation reasoning. Take a shortest closed geodesic in a nontrivial free homotopy class. The holonomy of parallel transport once around it is an isometry of the normal space; a dimension-parity argument guarantees it fixes some unit vector. Varying the geodesic in the direction of that parallel field shortens it because K positive makes the second variation negative, contradicting minimality. The conclusion splits by parity, and the real projective spaces show why the parity hypotheses cannot be dropped.

slides.title: Curvature Pinching and the Sphere Theorem
slides.notes: This is the capstone teaser. Bonnet-Myers and Synge constrain topology but do not pin down the manifold; the sphere theorem says that if curvature is positive and tightly pinched, the manifold must actually be a sphere. The classical topological version uses Toponogov comparison and Berger-Klingenberg injectivity-radius estimates. The pinching constant one-quarter is sharp, and the borderline example is complex projective space with the Fubini-Study metric, which is exactly quarter-pinched and is not a sphere. Mention the 2009 differentiable sphere theorem of Brendle and Schoen, proved with Ricci flow.

slides.title: Sign of Curvature: A Consequence Ledger
slides.notes: Use this ledger as the synthesis slide. Walk down the rows and emphasize the symmetry: as curvature moves from constant through nonpositive to strictly positive, the universal cover shrinks from one of three models, to contractible Euclidean space, to a compact manifold, and finally to the manifold itself. In lockstep the fundamental group moves from a free discrete quotient group, to infinite torsion-free, to finite, to trivial. The unifying mechanism is geodesic spreading governed by Jacobi fields.

slides.title: Recap: Curvature Writes Topology
slides.notes: Close by replaying the chapter as a single argument template. Local curvature feeds the Jacobi equation, the Jacobi equation decides whether conjugate points appear within a bounded distance, the conjugate-point behavior decides whether the universal cover is compact or contractible, and the cover's topology pins down the fundamental group. Killing-Hopf, Cartan-Hadamard, Bonnet-Myers, Synge, and the sphere theorem are five instances of that one pipeline run with different curvature inputs.
